data.content_ref: inline:The target claims to defend the preference for better-corroborated theories 'on Popper's own terms,' but its mechanism silently substitutes a different Popperian concept — boldness/empirical content — for corroboration. In Popper's framework these are distinct: a theory's degree of corroboration depends on the severity and number of tests it has survived, whereas its degree of boldness (empirical content, testability) is a property of the theory's logical form prior to testing. A theory can be maximally bold yet minimally corroborated (e.g., it makes many risky predictions, most of which narrowly escape falsification), or moderately bold yet highly corroborated (it has passed many severe tests). By equating 'better-corroborated' with 'highest empirical content,' the target's mechanism does not defend the preference Popper actually endorsed — for better-corroborated theories — but instead defends a preference for the boldest theory, which Popper would only endorse as a target for criticism, not as a preference for acceptance. This is a category substitution that breaks the claim's internal coherence: the defense succeeds only by redefining the object of preference.
